summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful in Peru since the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to those for rape. The age of consent is 14 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation under a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, applying equally to trans and cisgender youth. Trans identity is not itself an offence.

Discrimination and hate crimes on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity were criminalised by Government Decree Nº 1323, in effect 7 January 2017, through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code. Congress voted 66 to 29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition for removal carrying one million signatures; the repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members arguing the President lacked authority to issue the decree, but President Kuczynski's veto stood. The outcome nonetheless left Peru among three South American countries, alongside Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in practice. No protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of gender identity is currently in force.

Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, restricts trans people's use of public restrooms. Congress's committee approved unanimously, for plenary, the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 presented by Jorge Montoya of the Honor y Democracia party, and Congress approved bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR (sponsored by Muñante and Montoya), banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. The IDEHPUCP human-rights institute of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru states the restriction openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks; the institute cites Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, under which gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights, and quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons. The April 2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' separately mandates that public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people including trans youth from facilities matching their identity; its vague child-protection articles (article 4's media and advertising ban, article 5) enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and the obscenity minimum sentence rises from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating. These restrictions on restroom access constitute a state-imposed constraint on trans people's daily movements that could intensify hostile interactions in transit spaces.

Transgender Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published 8 November 2016, permitting gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law covering legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity was introduced 4 November 2016 and remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021.

In May 2024 the government decreed 'transsexualism' a mental health problem to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the Ministry of Health (MINSA) revised the term to 'gender discordance' for health-insurance classification purposes. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities also removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described by Human Rights Watch as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In May 2024 MINSA reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases. Conversion therapy is banned in Peru for medical professionals, a protection with specific relevance to trans and LGBTQ minors exposed to such practices.

A report of 22 July 2024 by Agencia Presentes finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans human-rights defender and journalist, stresses that recorded numbers are only a sub-registry. The report cites a 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study finding that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

On 19 December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. The judgment, issued after years of litigation, is Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court via the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. April 2025's NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order' or 'security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising. Public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with the oldest recorded march in 1984.

The 2016 national education curriculum includes information on sexual orientation, sex and gender issues, describing sexual orientation as the result of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice. Opinion polls show age-based variation: 18 to 24-year-olds (66%) were markedly more favourable toward homosexuals than the population overall (49%), and younger people showed higher approval of same-sex marriage (8.3% approval among Peruvians in 2010, higher among younger respondents).
tangentialFactors:
Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian congresswoman, telling her to 'go use the men's room', an episode illustrating the public hostility that accompanies the legislative restrictions.

Congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at the Instituto Nacional Materno Perinatal, and community demands recorded alongside the bathroom bills include HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
localsOnly:
The name-change route available to transgender Peruvians through the civil registry is a resident-facing procedure; the 2016 Constitutional Court reversal permits gender-marker change on national identity documents through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery, while the comprehensive Gender Identity Law introduced in November 2016 remained pending as of March 2021.

Residents also face the practical consequences of Law 32331 and the April 2025 sexual-integrity law in everyday facility access, and MINSA's June 2024 reclassification of 'transsexualism' as 'gender discordance' governs health-insurance coverage of trans healthcare.

Peru's Congress voted in May 2017 to strip the Penal Code's LGBT anti-discrimination provisions; the outcome left the country among three South American states without such coverage, and public institutions are described by Outright International as contributing to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination.
outOfScopeNotes:
The claim that the recorded hate-crime figures are a sub-registry is unresolved: the inventory gives no denominator, no per-capita comparison against Peru's general homicide rate, and no period over which the rise occurred, so the magnitude of trans-specific violence relative to background violence cannot be established from these sources.

Whether bills 6506/8457 and 6505/2023-CR were enacted, and how Law 32331 of 13 May 2025 relates to the April 2025 sexual-integrity law's restroom provision, is not resolved in the inventory; the sources describe committee approval, plenary approval and enactment at different points without a single consolidated statement of the operative text.

The status of the 2016 Gender Identity Law after March 2021, and whether the veto dynamics of the 2017 anti-discrimination repeal left Articles 46 and 323 operative in practice, are not sourced beyond the dates given.
